paragraphs: Private learning and online learning have a known qualitative connection: a concept class can be learned with differential privacy exactly when it can be learned online with a finite mistake bound. That equivalence concerns whether learning is possible. Turning a learner of one kind into the other can still require substantial additional data or computation.

This paper investigates the computational cost of such a conversion. Earlier work had shown that certain pure-private learners, including uniform or highly sample-efficient ones, could be converted efficiently into online learners. The authors ask whether an efficient conversion also exists for general pure-private learners whose sample requirements are polynomial.

Their answer is negative under the assumption that one-way functions exist. With that cryptographic assumption, the broader efficient conversion is impossible. The result separates qualitative learnability from computational efficiency: knowing that both forms of learning are possible does not establish that an efficient algorithm for one can be efficiently transformed into an algorithm for the other.
neurips-2020-a-computational-separation-.tldr: Assuming one-way functions exist, general pure-private learners with polynomial sample complexity cannot always be efficiently converted into online learners.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe how reliably a model should perform beyond its training examples. PAC-Bayes is a framework for obtaining such bounds while accounting for the learning algorithm and data distribution. That flexibility can yield tighter guarantees than bounds that treat an entire class of predictors uniformly.

The paper shows that this flexibility still has a fundamental limit. It examines linear classification in one dimension, a task known to require only O(log(1/δ)/ε) examples, where ε controls the desired error and δ controls the probability of failure. Despite that modest sample requirement, the authors show that a PAC-Bayes analysis cannot establish this learning guarantee.

More precisely, for any algorithm that learns these classifiers, there is a realizable distribution on which its PAC-Bayes bound becomes arbitrarily large. Realizability means that the classification task is compatible with a classifier in the chosen class. The result therefore identifies a limitation of the analytical framework even on a learnable problem; a loose bound need not indicate that the underlying learning task is difficult.
neurips-2020-a-limitation-of-the-pac-bay.tldr: Even one-dimensional linear classification can be easy to learn while resisting a useful PAC-Bayes guarantee.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to help a model handle data from a different environment. This paper studies an especially restrictive version: only one unlabeled example from the target environment is available during adaptation. That single example provides little evidence about the range of appearances the model may later encounter, making conventional adaptation approaches prone to failure.

Adversarial Style Mining couples a style-transfer module with the model performing the actual task. The style-transfer module repeatedly searches for stylized images around the available target example that are difficult for the current task model. As the task model changes, the search changes too, directing training toward styles that remain challenging.

This competitive interaction is intended to make both modules improve together while exposing the task model to potential variation in the largely unseen target domain. Experiments on cross-domain classification and segmentation benchmarks report state-of-the-art adaptation performance in the one-shot setting. The findings support using actively mined style variation to make more effective use of an extremely small amount of target data.
neurips-2020-adversarial-style-mining-fo.tldr: Adversarial Style Mining improves one-shot domain adaptation by generating stylized examples that challenge the current task model.

paragraphs: Graph embedding represents a graph in a geometric space so that machine learning models can use its structure. Many methods focus on preserving which graph elements are close to one another. This paper argues that doing so can preserve topological patterns along an embedding manifold while still distorting those patterns in the surrounding Euclidean space.

That distinction matters because a downstream model may have difficulty detecting a pattern that is preserved on a curved manifold but distorted in the space where it operates. The authors propose curvature regularization to encourage flatter embedding manifolds. They introduce an angle-based measure called ABS curvature and use it to develop three forms of regularization.

The regularizers are integrated into five established proximity-preserving embedding methods. Across two applications and a range of public graph datasets, the authors report significant empirical improvements. These results support treating the geometry of the embedding manifold as an additional design concern: preserving local proximity alone may leave useful graph structure difficult for subsequent models to recognize.
neurips-2020-curvature-regularization-to.tldr: Curvature regularization encourages flatter graph embeddings so that preserved graph patterns are easier for downstream models to detect.

paragraphs: DeepWDC addresses classification when inputs undergo severe perturbations. Its central choice is to represent both inputs and labels as probability measures, giving the method a distributional basis for handling the effects of altered data. The paper investigates this approach for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional inputs.

The method seeks an optimal label measure with diffusion invariance: the label distribution remains stationary over time and becomes equivalent to a Gaussian measure. It also minimizes the 2-Wasserstein distance between the optimal label measure and a Gaussian measure. This distance compares probability distributions, and the authors describe its minimization as reducing Wasserstein uncertainty.

Experiments report substantial accuracy improvements when DeepWDC is used with several deterministic classification baselines. The method also outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the evaluated data with perturbations such as rotations, impulse noise, and down-scaling. The stated findings support distributional representations and diffusion invariance as useful tools for classification under these disruptions, with evidence covering multiple kinds of input changes.
neurips-2020-deep-diffusion-invariant-wa.tldr: DeepWDC uses probability distributions, diffusion invariance, and Wasserstein distance to improve classification on perturbed 2D and 3D data.

paragraphs: Selecting the k highest or lowest scores is a common step in machine learning systems. However, a hard top-k selection creates a difficulty for gradient-based training: a small score change can abruptly change which items are selected. Implementations that swap indices also do not provide the gradients needed to train the surrounding model end to end.

The paper introduces SOFT top-k, a smooth approximation to this selection operation. It expresses the approximate selection as the solution of an entropic optimal transport problem. This gives the system a smoother relationship between input scores and selection outputs, making it possible to obtain useful gradients through the selection step.

The authors efficiently approximate those gradients using the transport problem's optimality conditions. They apply the operator to k-nearest neighbors and beam search, reporting improved performance in numerical experiments. The contribution is a way to incorporate an approximate top-k decision into gradient-based learning, allowing selection-dependent components to participate in training rather than leaving the hard selection step without a usable gradient.
neurips-2020-differentiable-top-k-with-o.tldr: SOFT top-k uses entropic optimal transport to approximate hard selection with an operation that supports gradient-based training.

paragraphs: An instruction-following navigation agent must relate language to an environment it is still discovering. It also needs to plan beyond its next move, explore effectively, and recover from mistakes. The paper presents Evolving Graphical Planner, or EGP, as a module for addressing these linked demands using raw sensory input.

EGP dynamically builds a graph representation as the agent acquires knowledge of the environment. It expands the local action space to support more flexible decisions and carries out planning on a proxy representation. Together, these components provide a mechanism for global planning while the agent's available understanding of the world continues to grow.

The authors evaluate the model on vision-and-language navigation with photorealistic images. Using pure imitation learning, it achieves a 53% success rate on the Room-to-Room test split and reports an improvement of up to 5% over previous architectures. The findings support the value of an evolving graph for connecting ongoing perception with longer-range navigation decisions in the evaluated task.
neurips-2020-evolving-graphical-planner-.tldr: EGP builds an evolving graph for global navigation planning and achieves 53% success on Room-to-Room using imitation learning.

paragraphs: A PI-explanation identifies feature values that are sufficient to support a classifier's prediction. It is subset-minimal: removing any included feature-value pair would destroy that sufficiency. This makes the explanation precise about which information can jointly establish a prediction, without requiring it to have the smallest size among all possible explanations.

Earlier exact methods for computing these explanations for Naive Bayes classifiers could require exponential time and space in the worst case. The paper shows that one PI-explanation can instead be computed in log-linear time. The same result extends beyond Naive Bayes to the broader class of linear classifiers.

The authors also provide a way to enumerate PI-explanations with polynomial delay, controlling the waiting time between successive explanations. That guarantee matters when a prediction admits several distinct sufficient explanations. Experiments demonstrate performance gains over earlier algorithms and investigate ways to assess heuristic explanation quality. Together, the results make exact sufficient explanations more computationally accessible for the classifier families studied.
neurips-2020-explaining-naive-bayes-and-.tldr: The paper computes one minimal sufficient explanation for a linear classifier in log-linear time and enumerates explanations with polynomial delay.

paragraphs: In a stochastic bandit problem, each option produces uncertain observations, and exploration helps estimate which options have high average outcomes. This paper studies the goal of identifying every option whose mean is within ε of the best mean. The desired output is therefore the complete set of sufficiently good options.

That objective matters when exploration is an initial screening stage. The abstract gives the example of carrying promising treatments into more expensive clinical trials: retaining all sufficiently good candidates preserves options whose eventual clinical effectiveness is still uncertain. Finding one strong candidate, a fixed number of candidates, or those above a predetermined threshold serves a different purpose.

The authors identify mathematical challenges specific to recovering all ε-good arms and introduce two algorithms to address them. They report strong empirical performance on a New Yorker Caption Contest dataset containing 2.2 million ratings and on a dataset evaluating hundreds of possible cancer drugs. These studies demonstrate the proposed methods on two distinct settings where selecting a set of promising alternatives is relevant.
neurips-2020-finding-all-epsilon-good-ar.tldr: The paper introduces two algorithms for finding every stochastic bandit option whose average outcome is within ε of the best.

paragraphs: Decentralized optimization distributes an optimization problem across participants with local objective functions. This paper develops a framework for designing primal methods in that setting, assuming the local functions are smooth and strongly convex. Those assumptions define the mathematical regime in which the framework and its convergence results apply.

The approach approximately solves a sequence of subproblems generated by an accelerated augmented Lagrangian method. Allowing approximate solutions is central to the construction: the framework organizes the larger optimization process around these inexact intermediate computations. It also provides a systematic derivation of established decentralized algorithms, including EXTRA and SSDA, connecting them through a common design approach.

Combining the framework with accelerated gradient descent yields a new primal algorithm with an optimal convergence rate matched by lower bounds. Experiments further demonstrate effectiveness on highly ill-conditioned problems, where optimization can be difficult. The contribution therefore combines a unifying way to derive decentralized algorithms with a new method whose theoretical rate reaches the stated benchmark for the setting.
neurips-2020-ideal-inexact-decentralized.tldr: IDEAL unifies decentralized optimization methods and yields an algorithm with an optimal convergence rate for smooth, strongly convex local objectives.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning trains an agent across tasks so it can learn new, related tasks more quickly. Training tasks are often designed to resemble the expected target tasks, and then all are used. This paper asks whether choosing among the available tasks can improve both learning speed and eventual target-task performance.

The authors propose an information-theoretic selection algorithm that balances two considerations. Selected tasks should be relevant enough to the target tasks, while also differing sufficiently from one another. This makes task selection a joint problem of usefulness and variety, rather than simply accepting the entire available collection as the training set.

The selection procedure operates on a given set of tasks regardless of how those tasks were generated. The authors reproduce several meta-reinforcement-learning experiments from prior work and report better final performance in every reproduced experiment. Their results show that appropriate selection can make training faster and more effective, supporting the idea that the composition of training experience is itself an important part of meta-learning.
neurips-2020-information-theoretic-task-.tldr: Information-theoretic task selection improves meta-reinforcement learning by choosing training tasks that combine target relevance with diversity.

paragraphs: A generative model assigns likelihoods to data, suggesting a straightforward way to flag unfamiliar inputs: reject examples with low likelihood. However, such models can sometimes assign higher likelihoods to out-of-distribution examples than to data resembling their training distribution. In those cases, a simple likelihood threshold can give misleading results.

This paper focuses on variational autoencoders, or VAEs. The authors observe that some detection methods proposed for deep generative models also fail when applied to VAEs. That observation motivates evaluating the detection score in the context of this particular model family, where existing approaches may not provide the intended separation between familiar and unfamiliar inputs.

The proposed alternative is Likelihood Regret, described as an efficient out-of-distribution score for VAEs. The authors benchmark it against existing approaches, and their empirical results suggest the best overall detection performance among the methods compared on VAEs. The stated contribution is therefore a VAE-focused detection score supported by comparative evidence, with the improvement expressed as an overall empirical finding.
neurips-2020-likelihood-regret-an-out-of.tldr: Likelihood Regret is an efficient VAE out-of-distribution score whose benchmark results suggest better overall detection than the compared alternatives.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents often finish training with fixed solutions that cannot adapt to new information or disruptions. This paper draws inspiration from synaptic plasticity, the biological capacity for connections to change with experience. It investigates whether learning rules can equip a network to keep organizing its own weights during an agent's lifetime.

The search optimizes synapse-specific Hebbian rules rather than directly optimizing network weights. Networks then begin with random weights and use the discovered rules to modify their connections through experience. The authors demonstrate this approach across reinforcement-learning tasks with different sensory modalities and more than 450,000 trainable plasticity parameters.

The learned rules enable navigation in a dynamic two-dimensional pixel environment. They also allow a simulated three-dimensional quadruped to learn to walk while adapting to morphological damage absent from training, without an explicit reward or error signal, in fewer than 100 timesteps. These findings demonstrate adaptive behavior in the tested systems by learning how weights should change, rather than supplying a fixed set of trained weights.
neurips-2020-meta-learning-through-hebbi.tldr: Searching for synapse-specific Hebbian rules enables randomly initialized networks to adapt during operation, including to unseen damage in a simulated robot.

paragraphs: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning, or MAML, aims to prepare a model for rapid adaptation to new tasks. Prior work has questioned its effectiveness when test tasks differ from training tasks, motivating methods that tailor the starting weights to each task. This paper investigates another part of the process: the updates performed during fast adaptation.

The proposed method, ALFA, uses a small meta-network to generate learning-rate and weight-decay coefficients at each adaptation step. The learning rate controls the size of a weight update, while weight decay regulates the weights. Learning these coefficients makes the update procedure adaptive instead of concentrating the meta-learning effort solely on the initialization.

Experiments support adaptive hyperparameters as an important ingredient in few-shot learning. The authors report that ALFA can outperform MAML even when adaptation begins from random weights. That finding shows how strongly the update rule can influence rapid learning in the evaluated setting, and motivates treating fast adaptation as a learnable component alongside the choice of starting parameters.
neurips-2020-meta-learning-with-adaptive.tldr: ALFA learns per-step learning rates and weight decay for fast adaptation, and can outperform MAML even from random initialization.

paragraphs: Explaining a neural network through human-understandable concepts raises two questions: are the concepts interpretable, and do they capture enough of the model's prediction behavior? This paper formalizes the second question through completeness. The definition assumes that scores for a complete set of concepts contain sufficient information about the model's prediction.

The authors develop a concept-discovery method that seeks a complete concept set while also encouraging interpretability. This brings coverage of the model's behavior into the discovery objective. They also introduce ConceptSHAP to assign importance to individual concepts, adapting game-theoretic ideas that account for concepts across sets rather than considering each one only in isolation.

Evaluation combines proposed metrics with user studies. It includes synthetic data with known concept explanations and real image and language datasets. The authors report evidence that the method finds concepts that are both interpretable and complete in explaining decisions. The contribution connects what people can understand about a concept with how sufficiently the overall concept set accounts for the network's behavior.
neurips-2020-on-completeness-aware-conce.tldr: The paper defines concept completeness, discovers interpretable concept sets, and introduces ConceptSHAP to explain their importance.

paragraphs: Online optimization requires a learner to make decisions as a problem unfolds. This paper studies a setting where each decision contributes a hitting cost and a switching cost that depends on the previous p decisions. The objective therefore includes memory of a sequence of past actions, extending Smoothed Online Convex Optimization.

The authors propose Optimistic Regularized Online Balanced Descent for this problem class. They establish a constant competitive ratio that does not depend on the dimension. A competitive ratio measures performance relative to an offline benchmark with knowledge of the full problem sequence, so the result provides a multiplicative guarantee despite the learner's online information constraints.

The paper also connects this optimization problem with online control under adversarial disturbances. Through that connection, the optimization method leads to a constant-competitive policy for a broad class of control problems. The significance is both algorithmic and structural: handling costs with memory offers a route to performance guarantees for systems whose control decisions face disturbances over time.
neurips-2020-online-optimization-with-me.tldr: An online optimization method with memory achieves a dimension-free constant competitive ratio and yields guarantees for adversarially disturbed control.

paragraphs: In a Stackelberg game, a leader commits to a strategy and a follower responds. A learning leader may query the follower's payoffs or best responses to determine its commitment. Those queries create an opportunity for manipulation: the follower can answer as though it had different payoffs, influencing the strategy the leader chooses.

The follower's challenge is to select deceptive payoffs that induce a favorable commitment. Its eventual benefit must be evaluated using its true payoffs, after it best responds to that commitment. Finding suitable reported payoffs is therefore an optimization problem involving both the leader's learning process and the follower's actual preferences.

Earlier work considered a simplified version with a finite payoff space. This paper addresses the more general problem and shows that the follower can efficiently compute optimal or near-optimal deceptive payoffs in various learning-interaction scenarios. The result establishes that, within those scenarios, effective manipulation is computationally attainable and need not depend on restricting the possible payoffs to a finite set.
neurips-2020-optimally-deceiving-a-learn.tldr: Followers can efficiently compute optimal or near-optimal deceptive payoffs in several Stackelberg learning scenarios beyond finite payoff spaces.

paragraphs: A targeted transfer attack constructs an adversarial image using a source classifier and aims to make another, blackbox classifier assign a chosen class. This paper investigates how to make such attacks transfer more effectively. Its focus is the hierarchy of internal image representations learned by deep neural networks.

The proposed framework perturbs representations at multiple layers so that they resemble other classes. This broadens the attack objective beyond changing the source model's final output decision. The framework supports flexible combinations of layer-level perturbations and achieves state-of-the-art targeted transfer performance between the ImageNet networks evaluated by the authors.

The paper also relaxes the usual assumption that source and target models share their training dataset and label space. Feature-space methods remain superior in those evaluations, with some instances showing a tenfold increase in targeted success rate relative to other transfer methods. The authors analyze why the methods outperform existing strategies and extend the approach to a setting permitting limited blackbox queries. These findings identify internal representations as useful targets for transferable adversarial perturbations.
neurips-2020-perturbing-across-the-featu.tldr: Perturbing multiple internal feature layers improves targeted attack transfer, including some settings with different source and target datasets or labels.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from earlier tasks to make learning a related task more data-efficient. However, many approaches assume that the training tasks have already been supplied or chosen randomly. This paper focuses on the process of obtaining that experience when tasks are collected sequentially and each new collection step has a cost.

The authors introduce task selection based on prior experience into a meta-learning algorithm. They describe both the learner and the active selection setting through a probabilistic latent-variable model. This formulation makes the choice of training tasks part of the learning process, allowing accumulated experience to inform what the learner studies next.

The approach is evaluated in simulated robotic experiments, where the authors provide empirical evidence of improved data efficiency relative to strong baselines. Robotics motivates the problem because physical data collection can cause wear and tear. The findings support actively choosing meta-training tasks as a way to use collected experience more effectively, alongside the usual goal of adapting efficiently after that experience has been acquired.
neurips-2020-probabilistic-active-meta-l.tldr: A probabilistic active meta-learning method uses prior experience to select training tasks and improves data efficiency in simulated robotics.

paragraphs: Sliced divergences compare probability distributions by projecting them onto random one-dimensional directions, measuring a base divergence in each projection, and averaging. This construction has proved useful in machine learning, including generative modeling. The paper examines which mathematical and statistical properties survive this reduction to one-dimensional comparisons.

The authors show that slicing preserves metric axioms and weak continuity of the divergence, allowing the sliced construction to retain related topological properties. These properties concern whether the comparison behaves like a distance and how it responds when distributions converge. They further specialize the analysis to base divergences belonging to the class of integral probability metrics.

On the statistical side, the paper establishes that sample complexity can be independent of the original problem dimension under mild conditions. This is a conditional result about estimating sliced divergences from data. The authors apply the general theory to several base divergences and illustrate it with synthetic and real-data experiments, providing a mathematical foundation for properties that make slicing useful in practice.
neurips-2020-statistical-and-topological.tldr: Slicing preserves key properties of probability divergences and, under mild conditions, yields dimension-independent sample complexity.

paragraphs: The paper studies minimax optimization: choosing x to minimize the largest value an opposing choice y can produce. The objective may be nonconvex in x but is strongly concave in y, whose feasible set is convex and compact. The algorithm has access only to unbiased stochastic gradient estimates, a setting relevant to robust optimization and adversarial training.

The goal is to find an approximately stationary point of the function obtained after maximizing over y. The authors introduce SREDA, a stochastic recursive gradient descent-ascent method that uses variance reduction to estimate gradients more efficiently. The target is stationarity of this maximized objective, reflecting the nonconvex structure of the minimization problem.

SREDA requires O(κ³ε⁻³) stochastic gradient evaluations, compared with O(κ³ε⁻⁴) for the stochastic gradient descent-ascent method described in the abstract. Here κ is the condition number and ε sets the accuracy scale. The authors establish optimal dependence on ε for this problem, improving how computational demand grows as a more accurate stationary point is requested.
neurips-2020-stochastic-recursive-gradie.tldr: SREDA uses variance reduction to achieve optimal accuracy dependence for stochastic nonconvex–strongly-concave minimax optimization.

paragraphs: When several players learn simultaneously, guarantees about accumulated regret do not directly describe the quality of their latest decisions. This paper studies last-iterate convergence, asking how quickly the current output of a learning algorithm approaches a solution. It considers smooth monotone games and measures progress using a gap function.

The authors show that optimistic gradient with a constant step size achieves an O(1/√T) last-iterate rate, while also being a no-regret algorithm. Here T is the number of iterations. Their proof introduces an adaptive potential function chosen at each iteration, providing a way to analyze the evolving learning process and establish the rate.

A matching lower bound shows that this rate is tight for the class of p-SCLI algorithms, which includes optimistic gradient. The optimality statement therefore applies within that algorithm class and the stated game setting. The lower-bound analysis also gives a more direct proof of an existing conjecture. Together, the results clarify both the attainable last-iterate guarantee and a boundary on improving it within the considered class.
neurips-2020-tight-last-iterate-converge.tldr: Optimistic gradient achieves an O(1/√T) last-iterate rate in smooth monotone games, matching a lower bound for its broader algorithm class.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks aim to reduce the resources needed to run large models. However, producing a sparse model can still involve dense parameters or dense gradients during training. Those intermediate requirements can make training prohibitively expensive even when the final model is sparse, especially as model sizes grow.

Top-KAST addresses this issue by maintaining constant sparsity throughout both the forward and backward passes. Its contribution concerns the training process as well as the resulting network. Keeping both passes sparse targets the dense computations or representations that otherwise remain a barrier to using sparse models at larger scales.

On ImageNet, the authors report performance comparable to or better than previous work while preserving sparsity. They also demonstrate the approach in language modeling, a domain where large architectures motivate resource-efficient alternatives. The method is described as straightforward to implement in existing machine learning frameworks with few additional lines of code. The findings support always-sparse training as a practical approach to exploring larger models with reduced resource requirements.
neurips-2020-top-kast-top-k-always-spars.tldr: Top-KAST maintains sparsity in both training passes while matching or exceeding prior ImageNet results and also supporting language modeling.

paragraphs: A transcompiler converts source code from one programming language to another. Traditional systems use handcrafted rewrite rules, but their output can be hard to read, depart from target-language conventions, or require manual correction. Neural translation offers another approach, although paired examples of equivalent programs in different languages are scarce.

The paper develops a fully unsupervised neural transcompiler using approaches from unsupervised machine translation. Training uses monolingual source code from open-source GitHub projects, without paired translations or source- and target-language expertise. The authors demonstrate function translation among C++, Java, and Python, and describe the method as readily generalizable to other languages.

To evaluate translations, they build and release a test set of 852 parallel functions with unit tests for checking correctness. The model translates functions with high accuracy and significantly outperforms the commercial rule-based baselines tested. These findings show that unpaired code collections can provide useful training material for program translation, reducing dependence on the parallel examples that have constrained neural approaches in this domain.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-translation-of.tldr: An unsupervised neural transcompiler learns from unpaired code and outperforms tested commercial rule-based systems on function translation.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows assign likelihoods to images, but those likelihoods can be misleading indicators of whether an image belongs to the training distribution. The paper highlights a striking example: a flow trained on clothing images can assign higher likelihood to handwritten digits. It investigates the mechanisms behind this behavior, focusing on flows built with coupling layers.

The authors demonstrate that these models learn local pixel correlations and broadly applicable transformations from images into latent space. Such patterns and transformations need not be specific to the intended image dataset. Consequently, an unfamiliar image can fit properties the flow has learned even when its semantic content differs from the training data.

By changing the architecture of coupling layers, the authors bias the model toward learning semantic structure specific to the target data and improve out-of-distribution detection. Their investigation also shows that properties supporting high-fidelity image generation can harm detection. The findings explain why a flow's ability to model or generate images does not by itself establish that its likelihood reliably identifies unfamiliar inputs.
neurips-2020-why-normalizing-flows-fail-.tldr: Coupling-layer flows can favor generic image statistics over dataset semantics, and architectural changes that encourage semantics improve out-of-distribution detection.
